WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a Democratic initiative that would have taxed the windfall profits oil companies have enjoyed due to rising energy prices, with the minority leader calling the proposal a "gimmick." Record energy prices have led to record profits for oil companies. The measure failed to achieve the 60 votes required by Senate rules to proceed. The vote was 51-43. Six Republicans, including three seeking re-election in November, broke ranks to support the bill. Two Democrats -- Sen. Mary Landrieu of oil-producing state Louisiana and Majority Leader Harry Reid, who voted no to be able to bring the measure back to the floor under Senate rules -- voted against the measure. Along with placing a special tax of 25 percent on oil companies, the bill would have permitted lawsuits against the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, the oil-producing cartel, and suspended deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Profits from renewable energy sources would be excluded from the tax. "We're not afraid, on this side, to go after Big Oil when they are not doing the right thing," said Sen. Charles Schumer, D-New York. "And we are not afraid to go after OPEC because they are a cartel that squeezes us. "We're not afraid to do some strong tough things that will -- some in the short run, some in the longer run -- that will bring down the price, the all too high price, of gasoline." Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-North Dakota, said the measure was needed to "wring out" speculators he blamed for driving the price of crude oil to more than $130 a barrel in recent weeks . But Senate Republicans insisted the new taxes ultimately would hurt consumers and cut American oil supply, saying Democrats simply were playing election-year politics. The bill is "pure and simple a pathetic attempt to even call itself an energy plan," said Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said, "Hitting the gas companies might make for good campaign literature or evening news clips, but it won't address the problem. This bill isn't a serious response to gas prices. It is just a gimmick." The Kentucky Republican added, "They are hoping the idea of going after energy companies will create the illusion of action after a week in which they themselves fought for a bill that would make the problem worse. What a political charade." As the average cost of gas edged above $4 a gallon, high prices are definitely on the minds of voters. A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll released Tuesday shows 40 percent of respondents are more concerned about the cost of gasoline than long lines at the pump, which occurred during the energy crisis of the 1970s. But 55 percent of those surveyed are more worried about the long lines and rationing. The poll results reflect telephone interviews with 1,035 adults on Wednesday and Thursday. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points. CNN's Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis and Scott J. Anderson contributed to this report.

***

### Senate Republicans Block Democratic Energy Bill Targeting "Big Oil" Profits Amid Surging Gas Prices

**WASHINGTON** — In a showdown reflecting deep-seated partisan divisions over national energy strategy, Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a major Democratic legislative package designed to crack down on major oil companies and provide relief to consumers grappling with record-high prices at the pump. 

The vote on the *Consumer-First Energy Act* ended 51–43, falling short of the 60-vote threshold needed to overcome a Republican filibuster and advance the measure to a full debate. The result effectively kills the centerpiece of the Democratic leadership's response to rising inflation and surging fuel costs.

#### A Three-Pronged Attack on Energy Costs

The proposed legislation arrived at a moment of intense political pressure, driven by public outrage over skyrocketing gasoline prices that have strained household budgets nationwide. At the same time, the world’s largest oil conglomerates—including ExxonMobil, Chevron, BP, and Shell—have reported quarterly earnings that shattered previous corporate records. 

To address what they characterized as corporate profiteering, Senate Democrats crafted a aggressive three-pronged legislative strategy:

1. **A 25 Percent Windfall Profits Tax:** The bill would have levied a 25 percent tax on the "unreasonable" profits of major integrated oil companies—specifically those producing more than 500,000 barrels of crude oil per day—that fail to reinvest their earnings into domestic oil production, refinery expansion, or renewable energy sources.
2. **Anti-OPEC Litigation:** The package contained a provision known as the No Oil Producing and Exporting Cartels (NOPEC) act, which would amend U.S. antitrust law to allow the Department of Justice to sue members of the OPEC cartel for price-fixing and market manipulation.
3. **Suspension of Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) Deposits:** To immediately increase commercial supplies on the open market, the bill called for a temporary halt on federal purchases of crude oil meant for the nation's emergency stockpiles.

#### Clashing Visions on Energy Policy

The floor debate showcased fundamental differences between the two parties regarding market regulation, corporate responsibility, and the root causes of energy crises.

Democrats framed the measure as a necessary defense of working-class families who are being squeezed at the pump while oil executives reap unprecedented windfalls. 

"American families are paying out the nose to fill their gas tanks, while Big Oil companies are rolling in record profits and handing out massive buybacks to their Wall Street investors," said one Senate Democratic sponsor during the debate. "This bill sends a clear message: the free ride for corporate greed is over. It’s time to put consumers first."

Republicans, however, fiercely opposed the bill, arguing that punitive taxes on energy producers would backfire by discouraging domestic investment, reducing supply, and ultimately driving gas prices even higher. Pointing to historic precedents, opponents referenced the windfall profits tax enacted during the Carter administration in 1980, which economic studies later showed decreased domestic oil production and increased reliance on foreign imports.

"You cannot tax your way to lower gas prices," said a leading Senate Republican. "Punishing domestic energy producers is a flawed, short-sighted gimmick that will stifle innovation, curb American production, and leave us even more reliant on foreign energy sources. If we want lower prices, the solution is simple: lease more federal land, cut red tape, and increase domestic supply."

#### Legislative Gridlock and What Lies Ahead

The 51–43 procedural vote largely fell along strict party lines, reflecting the deep ideological chasm in Congress over climate, energy, and tax policies. A handful of crossover votes were not enough to break the impasse. 

With the defeat of the legislation, the debate over how to handle energy costs shifts back to the executive branch and the election trail. Democrats are expected to continue highlighting corporate profits as a key driver of inflation ahead of the upcoming elections, while Republicans plan to keep the focus on current regulatory policies that they contend hinder American energy independence.

For the moment, however, the legislative stalemate guarantees that federal intervention into oil company profits remains off the table, leaving American drivers to navigate high gas prices without new policy relief from Capitol Hill.

**Senate Republicans block Democratic bill targeting 'windfall' oil profits amid pain at the pump**

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked a Democratic-led effort to impose a tax on the record profits of major oil companies, dealing a swift blow to President Joe Biden’s legislative agenda as Washington grapples with voter anger over soaring gas prices.

The measure, titled the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act, fell short of the 60 votes required to overcome a GOP filibuster, failing on a largely party-line vote. 

The legislative showdown caps weeks of escalating rhetoric on Capitol Hill, where Democrats have sought to pin the blame for record-high energy costs on corporate greed, while Republicans argue that the Biden administration’s climate policies have choked off domestic energy production.

### A fiery debate over corporate profits

Under the proposed bill, major oil companies that produce or import more than 300,000 barrels of crude oil per day would face a per-barrel tax equal to 50% of the difference between the current price of oil and the average price between 2015 and 2019. The revenue generated by the tax would have been returned directly to consumers in the form of a quarterly rebate.

Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer blasted oil executives on the Senate floor ahead of the vote, pointing to quarterly earnings reports that showed energy behemoths like ExxonMobil and Chevron pulling in tens of billions of dollars in profits.

"While American families are forced to make tough choices at the grocery store just to afford the gas to get to work, Big Oil is popping champagne and spending billions on stock buybacks," Schumer said. "This is not free-market capitalism; it is unadulterated price gouging, and it is time for Congress to intervene."

Democrats hoped the measure would provide tangible relief to voters struggling with inflation, a issue that poses a severe political threat to the party’s narrow control of Congress in the upcoming elections.

### Republicans warn of energy shortages

Republicans, however, united against the proposal, dismissing it as a "reckless tax-and-spend gimmick" that would ultimately backfire on consumers.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell argued that imposing new taxes on domestic energy producers would disincentivize exploration and drilling, leading to a further drop in supply and pushing pump prices even higher.

"The Democrats’ solution to a self-inflicted energy crisis is to hike taxes on the very companies we need to produce more energy," McConnell said during a morning press conference. "You cannot tax your way to lower gas prices. This is a punitive, socialist policy that will leave America more reliant on foreign oil from hostile nations."

GOP lawmakers pointed to the Carter-era windfall profits tax of 1980, citing Congressional Research Service studies showing that the historic tax decreased domestic oil production and increased reliance on foreign imports.

### The political calculus

Industry trade groups, including the American Petroleum Institute (API), aggressively lobbied against the bill, arguing that the industry's profits are cyclical and necessary to fund the massive capital investments required for future energy development.

Despite the bill’s failure, analysts say the vote serves a crucial political purpose for both parties. 

For Democrats, it creates a paper trail showing they attempted to hold corporate America accountable and offer direct checks to consumers. For Republicans, the vote allows them to double down on their messaging that the Democratic administration is fundamentally anti-fossil fuel.

With the bill now effectively dead for the session, the White House is expected to turn to alternative measures, including potential releases from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and renewed pressure on international energy cartel OPEC to boost production. 

However, with gas prices remaining near historic highs and gridlock entrenched in the Senate, relief for American drivers appears unlikely to come from Capitol Hill anytime soon.

Here is a summary of the event based on CNN's reporting and congressional records from **June 10, 2008**:

---

### **The Event: Senate Blocks the Energy Bill**
On June 10, 2008, Senate Republicans successfully blocked a Democratic-led energy bill—known as the **Consumer First Energy Act**—that aimed to impose a "windfall profits tax" on major oil companies and roll back billions in tax breaks for the industry.

* **The Vote:** The measure needed 60 votes to overcome a Republican procedural filibuster and move to a full vote. It failed on a **51–43 vote** (mostly along party lines).

---

### **Key Provisions of the Proposed Bill**
The Democratic bill aimed to penalize major oil companies for what supporters called "excessive profits" during an economic squeeze on American families. It proposed:

1. **Windfall Profits Tax:** A 25% tax on the "unreasonable" profits of major oil companies (such as ExxonMobil, Chevron, ConocoPhillips, BP, and Shell) unless those companies reinvested that money into renewable energy or domestic refinery expansion.
2. **Repeal of Tax Breaks:** Rolling back roughly **$17 billion** in tax subsidies and incentives previously granted to the top oil companies.
3. **OPEC Lawsuits:** Allowing the U.S. Department of Justice to sue OPEC member nations for price-fixing and cartel activity.
4. **Targeting Speculation:** Increasing regulation on Wall Street energy speculators, whom Democrats blamed for artificially inflating oil prices.

---

### **The Debate and Arguments**

#### **The Democratic Position (Pro-Tax)**
* **Argument:** Oil companies were making record-shattering profits (ExxonMobil alone reported a record $40.6 billion profit in 2007) while Americans were suffering at the pump.
* **Key Quote/Stance:** Senate Majority Leader **Harry Reid (D-NV)** argued that oil companies did not need government tax breaks while gas was over $4 a gallon, calling the subsidies "unnecessary corporate welfare." Democrats argued the tax revenue should be redirected toward renewable energy and consumer relief.

#### **The Republican Position (Anti-Tax)**
* **Argument:** Taxing oil companies would disincentivize domestic energy production, leading to *less* oil on the market and ultimately pushing gas prices even higher. They pointed to the 1980s windfall profits tax under President Jimmy Carter, which studies suggested reduced domestic oil production and increased reliance on foreign oil.
* **Key Quote/Stance:** Senate Minority Leader **Mitch McConnell (R-KY)** and President **George W. Bush** argued that the solution was to increase domestic supply by expanding offshore drilling and opening up parts of Alaska (ANWR) for exploration—coining the push for "Drill, Baby, Drill."

---

### **Context of the 2008 Gas Crisis**
* **Peak Prices:** Gas prices eventually peaked in July 2008 at a national average of **$4.11 per gallon** (equivalent to over $5.80 in today's dollars).
* **2008 Election Impact:** Gas prices were a central debate in the 2008 presidential race between **Barack Obama** (who supported taxing oil profits and investing in green energy) and **John McCain** (who favored lifting bans on offshore drilling).
* **Subsequent Crash:** Prices plummeted later in late 2008, dropping below $2.00 per gallon by the end of the year, due to the global financial crash and the onset of the Great Recession, which severely reduced global energy demand.

The defeat comes as gas prices cross an unprecedented national average of $4 a gallon, making energy costs the top economic concern for American families heading into the 2008 presidential election.

Under the proposed legislation, a 25 percent tax would have been levied on the profits of major foreign and domestic oil companies that failed to reinvest those earnings into clean energy technologies or domestic refining capacity. The bill also sought to revoke $17 billion in tax breaks for the industry and crack down on institutional speculation in the energy futures markets.

Democrats blasted Republicans for blocking the measure, accusing them of protecting corporate interests at the expense of struggling consumers.

"The American people don't want tax hikes that will worsen the crisis; they want more American energy. If we want to lower prices at the pump, we need to drill here, and we need to drill now."

"This bill is nothing more than a political gimmick designed to cover up the failure of the Biden administration's anti-energy agenda," McConnell said. "From day one, this administration has canceled pipelines, frozen new federal leasing, and discouraged investment in domestic fossil fuels. Now, when their own policies create a supply shortage, their solution is to punish the very companies we need to produce more energy. You cannot tax your way to lower gas prices."

Republicans cited historical precedent, pointing to the late 1970s and 1980s when the U.S. implemented a windfall profits tax on crude oil. Studies by the Congressional Research Service later found that the tax reduced domestic oil production by up to 8% and increased reliance on foreign oil imports.

GOP senators also argued that oil is a globally traded commodity whose price is set by worldwide supply and demand dynamics, not individual corporate boardrooms. They insisted that the solution to high energy costs lies in deregulation, streamlined permitting processes, and expanding American energy independence.

### Industry Reaction and Economic Outlook

The American Petroleum Institute (API), the primary trade group for the U.S. oil and gas industry, welcomed the Senate's rejection of the bill. In a statement released shortly after the vote, the API warned that penalizing success in the energy sector would deter the capital investment required to build new infrastructure and bring more energy to market.

"Taxing American energy production at a time when the world needs more supply is counterproductive," the statement read. "The focus should be on policies that encourage domestic production and infrastructure growth, not punitive measures that threaten economic growth and national security."

Independent economists remain divided on the efficacy of windfall profit taxes. While some argue the rebates would provide immediate relief to low-income households, others warn that the tax structure could discourage companies from making long-term investments in high-risk exploration projects.

With the bill now defeated, both parties are expected to make energy prices a centerpiece of their upcoming campaign messaging. Democrats plan to continue highlighting corporate earnings reports to rally their base, while Republicans vow to press for executive actions that open up more federal lands for oil and natural gas production. 

For everyday consumers, however, the legislative stalemate means relief at the pump will remain subject to the volatile forces of the global energy market rather than action from Capitol Hill.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a realistic news article from June 2008 about Congress trying to address $4-a-gallon gasoline prices through oil industry taxes and lawsuits against OPEC?
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON** — With national gasoline prices shattering the $4-a-gallon mark for the first time in history, Democratic leaders in Congress launched an aggressive legislative offensive this week targeting major oil companies and foreign oil cartels.

Faced with mounting public anger and a slowing economy, the Democratic-led Senate moved forward on a pair of contentious bills aimed at curbing record energy costs. The measures seek to strip billions in tax subsidies from the world's largest oil companies, levy a windfall profits tax, and open the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) to federal antitrust lawsuits.

According to AAA, the national average for a gallon of regular unleaded hit a record $4.05 on Wednesday, up more than a dollar from a year ago. Crude oil futures briefly touched $138 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange earlier this week, driven by surging global demand, a weakening U.S. dollar, and market speculation.

"The American people are hurting, and they want action," Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) said during a Capitol Hill news conference. "We cannot stand by while Big Oil pockets tens of billions of dollars in profits every quarter while working families are forced to choose between filling up their gas tanks and buying groceries."

The proposed Consumer Energy Supply Act would repeal roughly $17 billion in tax breaks over ten years for the top five major oil companies—including ExxonMobil, Chevron, and ConocoPhillips—and redirect those funds toward renewable energy development and energy efficiency programs. It would also impose a 25 percent tax on "unreasonable" profits of major producers that do not reinvest their earnings into new domestic refining capacity or clean technology.

Simultaneously, lawmakers are pushing the "No Oil Producing and Exporting Cartels" Act, commonly known as NOPEC. The legislation would revoke the sovereign immunity that currently protects foreign nations from legal action in U.S. courts, allowing the Department of Justice to sue OPEC member nations for illegal price-fixing and market manipulation.

"For decades, OPEC has operated as an illegal price-fixing cartel, holding the global economy hostage," said Sen. Charles Schumer (D-N.Y.), a chief sponsor of the NOPEC bill. "It is time to hold these foreign nations accountable under the same antitrust laws that apply to every other business operating in the United States."

However, both measures face fierce resistance from congressional Republicans, the Bush administration, and the oil industry, setting up a major political showdown five months before the presidential election.

Republicans argue that taxing oil companies will discourage domestic production, leading to lower supply and even higher prices at the pump. Instead, GOP lawmakers are pressing to open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR) and restricted offshore areas to expanded oil drilling.

"You do not lower the price of gas by raising taxes on the people who produce it," said Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.). "If Congress wants to lower prices, we need to increase domestic supply. The Democrats' solution is to tax, sue, and hope for the best, while continuing to block American energy production."

The White House issued a strong veto threat against both bills. Administration officials warned that attempting to sue OPEC could backfire, risking retaliatory action from foreign energy exporters or a sudden disruption in oil supplies. Energy Secretary Samuel Bodman argued that market forces—namely constrained supply and booming demand in emerging economies like China and India—are driving prices, not a conspiracy by producers.

Industry representatives also pushed back forcefully against the congressional proposals.

"Targeting American oil and gas companies with punitive taxes will only reduce the capital available for the massive investments needed to find and produce new energy resources," said Red Cavaney, president of the American Petroleum Institute. "It is an election-year quick fix that will cause long-term harm to American energy security."

The political battle comes as high energy prices drag on the broader U.S. economy, which is already reeling from the subprime mortgage crisis and a severe credit crunch. Airlines are cutting flights, trucking companies are struggling under the weight of $4.70-a-gallon diesel, and retailers report that consumers are curtailing discretionary summer travel.

Despite the veto threats and slim margins in the Senate, Democratic leaders say they intend to force votes on the oil tax and OPEC measures by the end of the month, eager to put Republicans on record ahead of the November election. Presumptive Democratic presidential nominee Barack Obama has endorsed the windfall profits tax, while Republican nominee John McCain has voiced opposition to the tax, calling instead for a temporary pause on the federal gas tax.

As the political debate drags on, drivers across the country express little optimism for near-term relief.

"I used to spend $40 to fill my truck, now it’s almost $90," said Marcus Vance, a contractor from Woodbridge, Virginia, as he filled up at a Sunoco station. "Congress can sue OPEC or tax Exxon all they want, but unless the price on that sign comes down, none of it matters to me."
